grades.quote: If the thread has recently been running a lot, it will have a priority substantially lower than its base priority. If the thread has not run for a long time (because it has been waiting for the user, for example), then its priority will equal the base priority. That way, a thread that wakes up after a long waiting period will take priority over a thread that has been able to run.
grades.reason: Directly explains how recent CPU usage lowers priority while waiting restores it, favoring a newly awakened thread.
The exercises do not explain decay-usage scheduling or its treatment of waking threads.

grades.quote: That way, it will get to run soon but not for much longer than usual. This is similar to the effect achieved through dynamic priority adjustments in decay usage schedulers and Microsoft Windows. As with those adjustments, the goal is not proportional sharing, but responsiveness and throughput.
grades.reason: Explains the responsiveness and throughput rationale through a CFS comparison, but not the recent-usage decay mechanism itself.

grades.quote: As soon as the disk transaction is complete, the scheduler should switch the processor’s attention to the virus scanner. That way, the virus scanner can quickly look at the data that was read in and issue its next read request, so that the disk drive can get back to work without much delay.
grades.reason: Explains why favoring a thread returning from an I/O wait improves throughput, but does not explain how recent CPU usage determines priority.
